title: Drop the stretch that went negative
hook: Nine days of gains and losses. Find the best run without trying every pair.

doesNotKnow: that a negative running total can be thrown away

misconception: To find the best stretch of days you must check every start and end pair.
objective: The learner can explain that a stretch whose total has gone negative can only drag down what follows, so starting over there never loses the best stretch, and one pass over 9 days finds the same best (6) as checking all 45 stretches.

claims.text: Nine days make 45 stretches of consecutive days (9 x 10 / 2), and the biggest total over any of them is 6, from days 4 to 7 (4 - 1 + 2 + 1); no other stretch reaches 6.
claims.source: Builder's node script over all start-end pairs of -2 1 -3 4 -1 2 1 -5 4: 45 pairs, maximum 6, achieved only at days 4-7. The stage's triangle is the same brute force (PAIR in Demo.tsx). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Own node brute force (fc19b6/kad.mjs): 45 pairs, max 6, unique at days 4-7.

claims.text: The line that never starts over (running total -2 -1 -4 0 -1 1 2 -3 1) never gets above 2.
claims.source: Builder's node script: cumulative sums of -2 1 -3 4 -1 2 1 -5 4 are -2, -1, -4, 0, -1, 1, 2, -3, 1; maximum 2. The same line is drawn on the stage as 'Kept everything'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Own cumulative sums -2 -1 -4 0 -1 1 2 -3 1; max 2.

claims.text: Starting over whenever the running total is below 0 gives running totals -2 | 1 -2 | 4 3 5 6 1 5 (start-overs after day 1 and after day 3), and the best total on the way is 6.
claims.source: Builder's node script, one pass with reset when the total is below 0: totals -2, then 1, -2, then 4, 3, 5, 6, 1, 5; best 6, matching the 45-pair maximum (c1). A walk by the learner with different start-overs can end lower; the reveal quotes the start-overs the learner actually made on a walk that reached 6 (any walk reaching 6 must start over after day 3). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Own reset-below-0 pass: -2 | 1 -2 | 4 3 5 6 1 5, best 6; matches advance() auto rule in Demo.tsx. 6 is only at days 4-7, so any walk reaching 6 restarts after day 3.

claims.text: A stretch whose total has gone negative can only drag down what follows, so dropping it never loses the best stretch.
claims.source: If the stretch so far sums to a negative number T, any stretch that continues it has total T + (rest) < rest, so starting fresh right after it is always at least as good. This is the correctness argument for Kadane's algorithm; also exercise 4.1-5 in CLRS 3rd edition (2009; linear-time maximum subarray; the maximum-subarray section is not in the 4th edition). Edition added 2026-10-14 by the builder per the pass-19 note. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Derivation re-done: T < 0 implies T + rest < rest. Note: CLRS exercise 4.1-5 is the 3rd edition numbering; the maximum-subarray section is not in CLRS 4e. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 20): Pass 20 source audit: search results (walkccc CLRS solutions, SLU course notes, Rutgers ch. 4 solutions) confirm 3e exercise 4.1-5 is the nonrecursive linear-time maximum-subarray exercise; 4e chapter 4 listings run 4.1 Multiplying square matrices to 4.7 Akra-Bazzi, with no maximum-subarray section. Derivation unchanged and still sound. Source correct.

claims.text: One pass over the days replaces checking all 45 stretches; this is Kadane's algorithm.
claims.source: Bentley, 'Programming Pearls: Algorithm Design Techniques', CACM 27(9), 1984, credits Kadane for the linear-time scan; CLRS exercise 4.1-5 asks for the linear-time solution. Builder's node check: the one-pass best equals the brute-force best for this list (6) and for 20,000 random lists. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Own check: one-pass equals brute force on this list and 50,000 random lists (0 mismatches). Bentley, CACM 27(9) 1984, credits Kadane.

recall.question: Running total of daily gains: it is -3 after a few days. What does the best-run scan do?
options: Starts over: this stretch can only drag down what follows
Keeps going: the next days might make up for it
Goes back and tries every earlier start
recall.why: A negative total added to any continuation makes it smaller, so starting fresh is at least as good. That is why one pass is enough.

references.note: Maximum-subarray problem; exercise 4.1-5 gives the linear-time scan
